strengths: Identifies and rigorously diagnoses a previously unsolved problem: naive joint training of an inverse dynamics model (IDM) with a pretrained video-generation world model collapses, and provides a clear, well-supported hypothesis (representation misalignment) backed by controlled experiments varying IDM/WM initialization (Fig. 2).

The proposed warm-up + end-to-end joint training solution is simple, well-motivated, and its effect on stabilizing codebook utilization/entropy is convincingly demonstrated across different warm-up lengths (Fig. 3).

Extensive multi-faceted evaluation: video prediction quality across 4 datasets, downstream real-action adaptation to OOD environments (LIBERO, RoboDesk), visual planning on the VP2 benchmark, codebook collapse analysis under real-action adapters, and ablations isolating the two directions of co-evolution (WM as tutor for LAM, LAM as control interface for WM).

Additional robustness checks in the appendix (different video backbone Wan2.1, model-size and data-scale scalability studies, compute-cost accounting) strengthen the generality claims and partially address efficiency concerns.
Reasonably detailed implementation and training descriptions (Appendix B/C) that aid reproducibility.
Clear qualitative evidence (action transfer visualizations) suggesting the learned latent action space transfers semantically across embodiments better than the two-stage baseline.
weaknesses: The core quantitative improvements in Table 1 (video prediction quality) are numerically small (e.g., PSNR/SSIM differences often <0.5, FVD differences ~10-15 points) despite added architectural/training complexity, raising questions about the practical magnitude of the contribution.

Linear probing results in Table 5, meant to directly assess latent action quality, show mixed/inconsistent results between JOINT and 2-STAGE (JOINT wins on some datasets, loses on others, e.g., LIBERO), which weakens the claim that joint training produces a 'higher-quality latent action space' based on this metric alone; the paper acknowledges this but pivots to downstream metrics without fully reconciling the discrepancy.

Visual planning success rates (Tables 3 and 4) are low in absolute terms across all methods (often <35%), making it hard to assess practical significance of the reported relative gains, and only 5 seeds are used without reported variance/error bars.

No statistical significance testing (confidence intervals, multiple seeds) is reported for the main video-prediction and adaptation tables, making it difficult to assess whether the modest gains are robust or within noise.

The explanation of why joint training with frozen-vs-pretrained world model differs (world model 'ignoring' uninformative gradients) is intuitive but not rigorously validated theoretically or with additional controlled probes beyond the codebook metrics.

Comparisons are limited mostly to an internally implemented two-stage baseline; comparisons to other recent competitive methods (e.g., Motus, AdaWorld) are only partial (AdaWorld appears only in the visual planning comparison, not in the main video-prediction benchmark), limiting the breadth of external validation.

Training budgets (30-60K steps) are modest relative to typical large-scale video generation training, so it's unclear whether the observed trends (e.g., co-evolution benefits) persist at the much larger scales likely needed for real-world deployment.

The related-work section cites two 'concurrent submissions' with placeholder author names/filenames (AC-LAM, MVP-LAM), which is unusual and could reflect an anonymization or citation-practice issue that reviewers should note, though it does not appear to be central to soundness.
